title: Redwood structured output & function-calling demo
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a 46-minute demo focused on structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool calling. Covered API and Console flows, schema enforcement, guardrails, and security considerations (VPC, KMS, SOC 2). Customer expressed interest in a POC to validate latency and cost; next steps agreed around pricing, security docs, and a benchmark session.
next_steps: Maya to send pricing and dedicated vs hosted comparison
Liam to share benchmark spreadsheet and sample schema prompts
Schedule POC benchmark session w/ Corvus engineering
Customer to share dataset and success criteria
action_items: Maya Chen: Send pricing deck and dedicated vs hosted comparison - due 2026-03-27
Liam O'Connor: Share benchmark spreadsheet and sample schema-based prompt set - due 2026-03-26
Priya Singh: Provide sample dataset and success criteria for POC - due 2026-04-01
Dana Holt: Request SOC2/HIPAA and KMS whitepaper from Redwood and confirm any gaps - due 2026-03-28
transcript: [00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE, and with me is Liam our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya: Good, thanks. Excited to see the structured output demo. We want to make sure we can get deterministic JSON back for downstream systems.
[00:16] Liam: Great, that's exactly what we're demoing today - JSON mode, schema enforcement, and function calling for tool integrations. We'll show both the API and Console experiences.
[00:26] Marco: Quick note from our side - latency and cost are big drivers. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated for predictable throughput. Also curious about KMS and VPC options.
[00:38] Maya: Totally. We'll cover those. Quick agenda: 1) API JSON mode, 2) Console structured output UI, 3) function/tool calling patterns, 4) guardrails and security, then next steps. Sound good?
[00:48] Priya: Yep.

[00:50] Liam: Ok starting the API walkthrough - here is a simple call in JSON mode. You provide a schema, the model returns structured JSON that we validate server-side. Example payload -> schema for product extraction.
[01:10] Marco: Are you doing strict validation or just best-effort sanitization? We can't have malformed JSON hitting downstream ETL jobs.

[01:18] Liam: We support strict schema enforcement. If output doesn't match, you get an error + model output. We also provide rerun hooks and a 'repair' suggestion. There's an option to auto-cast types, but you can turn that off.
[01:32] Priya: Nice. How do functions fit in? We want to call internal tools after parsing - like enrichment services.

[01:38] Liam: Function calling maps directly. You can define a function spec, Redwood will populate args from the parsed JSON and invoke the function or provide a signed payload for your service. We demo a mock enrichment call in the Console now.

[02:00] [screen share: Redwood Console] Liam: Here is the Console flow. You can flip on 'JSON mode', upload a JSON schema, toggle strictness, and preview sample completions. This preview helps you iterate on schema fields and guardrails.
[02:22] Dana: On the security side, if function calling triggers a backend invocation, is that routed through our VPC? We need data not to leave our network for PII-sensitive flows.

[02:31] Liam: For Private deployments and Dedicated, you can route function invocations through customer-managed networking. We also support signed webhooks and mutual TLS for the invocation path. For hosted, we offer an option where payloads can be encrypted with your KMS - we call that envelope encryption.
[02:48] Priya: You mentioned KMS - do you integrate with AWS KMS and other HSMs?
[02:53] Maya: Yes, AWS KMS, Google KMS, and customer HSM via partners. We'll include the KMS whitepaper in the follow-up.
[03:02] Marco: What about rate limiting and batching? Our workload has lots of short messages; batching could improve costs but might hurt latency.

[03:10] Liam: Exactly - Redwood Optimize suggests batching heuristics. You can set latency SLOs per route; the runtime does continuous batching within those SLOs. For strict low-latency paths, you can set max batch windows to near-zero.
[03:25] Priya: Any notes on KV cache with structured output? If we feed in conversation prefixes, will KV cache cause schema drift?

[03:32] Liam: The runtime manages KV cache separately from structural parsing. You can opt in to clear prefix caching per route. In practice we saw no schema drift when using JSON mode because the parser is strict and validator runs post-output.

[03:46] [05:00] Maya: Switching to a function-calling example - we ask the model to output a JSON payload with 'action' and 'params'. If action == 'enrich', Redwood triggers the enrichment function with params as args. Here's a simulated demo.

[05:20] [05:35] Liam: Note, transcription and some of the demo shell might look like 'functionCalling' in logs. Our logs include request/response hashes and the resolved function args for debugging - redacted by default in hosted logs but available in Dedicated/Private per audit settings.
[06:02] Priya: How are you handling hallucinations in structured fields? If model invents an ID or misspells, how do we guard?

[06:10] Liam: We have several layers: schema validation, value constraint lists (enumerations), and a checklist of post-validators you can register. Also quality monitoring hooks in Redwood Optimize that alert on schema regression stats tied to prompt sets.
[06:31] Marco: For POC, we need to measure both 99th-percentile latency and cost per 1k tokens. Can you run a benchmark with our sample data?
[06:38] Maya: Yes, Liam will own the benchmark templates. We'll run both hosted and Dedicated configs to show unit economics. We'll include network egress assumptions in the sheet.
[06:51] Liam: I'll drop the benchmark spreadsheet link in the follow-up: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/corvus-poc
[07:00] Priya: Cool. One more - how deterministic is the JSON output on repeated runs? We need reproducible parses for downstream diffs.

[07:07] Liam: With strict mode + temperature 0 and pinned model/version, we saw deterministic outputs for structured extraction tasks. Redwood also supports response hashing and stable rollouts so you can lock a model for the POC.
[07:20] Dana: From compliance - we need SOC 2 artifacts and must understand retention on hosted logs.

[07:26] Maya: We'll share SOC 2 report, data retention options, and the logging matrix. On hosted the default is 30 days for debug logs but you can opt into longer retention or send logs to your SIEM via syslog/stackdriver.
[07:40] Marco: Are there any known limitations with certain model architectures for function calling or JSON mode?

[07:46] Liam: Older smaller models may struggle with complex nested schemas. We recommend larger decoder models or our curated model profiles. The runtime also picks optimized kernels; sometimes quantized variants need more validation cycles.
[07:59] Priya: Could you demo a schema with nested arrays? We have nested product bundles in our dataset.

[08:05] Liam: Sure - live demo: here's a schema with 'bundles' as array of objects. I'm going to run a few examples. (typing) Output looks good, it's validated and returned as JSON. The Console preview shows the exact field mapping.
[08:30] [08:45] Priya: There's a small glitch in the preview - the console shows 'KV cahce' spelled wrong in the help text, minor doc bug, haha.
[08:53] Maya: Thanks, we'll file that doc issue. Good catch.
[09:00] Marco: On rollout - if we change schema or model, do you support canarying?

[09:06] Liam: Yes, per-route rollouts: canary, A/B, and automatic rollback on quality regression. Redwood Optimize can tie evaluation prompts to alerting so you don't accidentally degrade parsing accuracy.
[09:20] Priya: For function calling authentication, can we use SAML/OIDC to exchange identity?
[09:26] Maya: We support SAML/SSO for the Console and OIDC tokens for API-level auth. For service-to-service invocation we support mTLS and signed JWTs integrated with your IdP.
[09:38] Dana: Any concerns re: PII - can we ensure redact on logs?
[09:43] Liam: Yes, log redaction rules can be customer-configured. For Private deployments you can route logs to your own collectors and enforce redaction at the source.

[09:53] [10:10] Maya: Ok wrapping toward next steps - we recommend a 2-week POC: week 1 onboarding + small benchmark, week 2 scale up and regression checks. Liam will share prompts and the benchmark template.
[10:25] Priya: Sounds reasonable. Timeline wise we want results before end of April.
[10:30] Maya: Noted - we'll aim for initial benchmarks by 2026-04-10. Action items we'll include in the follow-up email. I'll also attach the security pack and pricing tiers.
[10:40] Marco: Anything else we should know about costs for function calls vs embedded outputs?
[10:46] Liam: Function calls are priced like normal API calls plus a small invocation fee if routed through Dedicated function runtimes. We'll share unit economics in the pricing doc.
[10:55] Priya: Can you include a sample of schema-based prompts and a baseline eval metric you use to compare runs?
[11:02] Liam: Yes, sample prompts + evaluation harness will be in the benchmark sheet. We also include historical baselines for similar customers.
[11:12] Dana: One more compliance ask: can Redwood sign an addendum around data processing for our enterprise contract?
[11:17] Maya: Our legal team has standard DPA and addendum templates. I'll loop them in once you confirm interest post-demo.
[11:26] [11:40] Priya: Great - thanks. This was helpful, the structured output + function calling flow looks like it could fit our needs.
[11:46] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send the follow-up with links: Deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/structured-output-demo and Benchmarks: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/corvus-poc
[11:59] Marco: Thanks, talk soon.
[12:03] [12:10] End of recording
